title: Mayflower Compact
description: Pilgrims aboard the Mayflower signed a self-governing agreement establishing a democratic colony in Plymouth.
cause: The Pilgrims had no legal authority to settle in the area and needed a governing framework to maintain order.
effect: Established an early precedent for self-governance and majority rule in the American colonies.
causes: Pilgrims lacked a royal charter for their landing site
Fear of mutiny without a governing structure
effects: Created a precedent for written self-government in North America
Majority-rule principle influenced later colonial governance
significance: One of the first examples of self-governance in North America
Foreshadowed the democratic principles embedded in the Constitution

title: Navigation Acts
description: England enacted mercantilist laws requiring colonial trade to flow through English ships and ports.
cause: England sought to consolidate economic control over its colonies and exclude Dutch traders.
effect: Fueled resentment in the colonies and contributed to a tradition of smuggling and resistance to British authority.
causes: England wanted to profit from colonial trade under mercantilism
Competition with Dutch shipping threatened English commercial dominance
effects: Colonial smuggling became widespread
Planted seeds of resentment toward British economic control
significance: Embodied mercantilist imperial policy toward the colonies
Created long-term colonial grievances that contributed to the Revolution

title: Bacon's Rebellion
description: Nathaniel Bacon led armed Virginia colonists against Governor Berkeley and Native Americans on the frontier.
cause: Frontier settlers were angered by Berkeley's refusal to protect them from Native American raids and by elite political control.
effect: Led planters to shift from indentured servants to enslaved Africans as a more controllable labor force.
causes: Elite political corruption under Governor Berkeley
Frustrated indentured servants with no land access after completing service
effects: Planters shifted to enslaved African labor to avoid future rebellions by freed servants
Revealed deep class tensions in colonial Virginia
significance: Pivotal turning point accelerating the growth of race-based slavery in Virginia
Demonstrated the dangers of a large class of discontented, landless colonists

title: Glorious Revolution / English Bill of Rights
description: England's Protestant monarchs William and Mary accepted parliamentary supremacy, reshaping colonial charters.
cause: Protestant opposition to the Catholic King James II forced his abdication.
effect: Strengthened colonial assemblies and reinforced the concept of constitutional limits on government power.
causes: Protestant fears of Catholic rule under James II
Parliament sought supremacy over the monarchy
effects: Colonial assemblies gained more independence from royal governors
Established constitutional monarchy as England's governing model
significance: Reinforced the idea that government authority derives from law, not divine right
Influenced the political philosophy behind the American Revolution

title: Salem Witch Trials
description: A wave of witchcraft accusations in Salem, Massachusetts led to twenty executions.
cause: Social tensions, religious anxiety, and political instability in Puritan Massachusetts created a climate of fear.
effect: Weakened the authority of Puritan clergy and prompted greater skepticism of spectral evidence in courts.
causes: Social and economic tensions between Salem Village and Salem Town
Political instability after the revocation of the Massachusetts Bay Charter
effects: Discredited use of spectral evidence in legal proceedings
Accelerated decline of Puritan theocratic authority in New England
significance: Illustrated the dangers of religious extremism and mob mentality
Marked a turning point toward greater legal rationalism in the colonies

title: French and Indian War
description: Britain and its colonial allies defeated France and its Native allies in a conflict over North American territory.
cause: Competing British and French territorial claims in the Ohio River Valley escalated into open warfare.
effect: Britain gained vast territory but accumulated massive debt, leading to new colonial taxes that sparked revolution.
causes: French expansion into the Ohio River Valley threatened British colonists
Both empires sought dominance over the lucrative fur trade
effects: Britain doubled its territorial holdings in North America
War debt prompted Britain to tax the colonies, igniting the Revolution
significance: Transformed North American politics by eliminating French power east of the Mississippi
Directly triggered the taxation disputes that led to American independence

title: Stamp Act
description: Britain imposed a direct tax on printed materials in the colonies to help pay war debts.
cause: Britain needed revenue after the French and Indian War and believed colonists should help pay for their defense.
effect: United colonial opposition under the 'no taxation without representation' slogan and led to the Stamp Act Congress.
causes: Britain's £140 million war debt after the French and Indian War
British belief that colonists should contribute to their own defense costs
effects: Sparked colonial boycotts of British goods
Led to the first intercolonial political body, the Stamp Act Congress
significance: First direct internal tax on colonists, violating their tradition of self-taxation
Crystallized the 'no taxation without representation' principle

title: Boston Massacre
description: British soldiers fired into a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people.
cause: Tensions between Boston residents and British troops stationed in the city had been escalating for months.
effect: Inflamed anti-British sentiment; Paul Revere's engraving became a powerful piece of revolutionary propaganda.
causes: Resentment over the Quartering Act forcing colonists to house British troops
Economic tensions caused by the presence of soldiers competing for jobs
effects: Paul Revere's propaganda engraving shaped colonial public opinion against Britain
Accelerated the push toward colonial independence
significance: Turned a street brawl into a rallying symbol for colonial resistance
Demonstrated the power of print media in shaping political opinion

title: Boston Tea Party
description: Colonial protesters dumped 342 chests of British East India Company tea into Boston Harbor.
cause: The Tea Act gave the East India Company a monopoly and colonists protested taxation without representation.
effect: Prompted Britain to pass the Intolerable Acts, which further unified colonial resistance.
causes: The Tea Act threatened colonial merchants by granting a monopoly to the East India Company
Colonists rejected Parliament's right to tax them without representation
effects: Britain responded with the Coercive (Intolerable) Acts, closing Boston Harbor
Twelve colonies sent representatives to the First Continental Congress
significance: Transformed protest from economic boycott to direct political defiance
Brought colonies closer to unified resistance against British authority

title: Declaration of Independence
description: The Second Continental Congress formally declared the thirteen colonies independent from Britain.
cause: Escalating military conflict, failed petitions to the Crown, and Enlightenment ideas inspired the break.
effect: Established Enlightenment principles—equality, natural rights, consent of the governed—as the foundation of American political thought.
causes: Continued military conflict after Lexington and Concord
Thomas Paine's Common Sense shifted public opinion toward independence
effects: Established Enlightenment ideals of natural rights as the basis of American government
Provided a framework for evaluating American democracy across history
significance: Articulated a universal theory of human rights that influenced revolutions worldwide
Remains the founding statement of American political identity

title: Articles of Confederation Ratified
description: The first U.S. constitution created a weak central government with most power reserved to the states.
cause: States feared a powerful central government after their experience under British rule.
effect: Proved inadequate for governing the new nation, leading to the Constitutional Convention of 1787.
causes: States feared that a strong central government would replicate British tyranny
Revolutionary ideology emphasized local self-governance
effects: Congress could not tax, regulate commerce, or enforce laws effectively
Shays' Rebellion exposed the weakness of the national government
significance: First attempt at national self-governance in America
Its failures directly led to the creation of the stronger Constitution of 1787

title: U.S. Constitution Ratified
description: Nine states ratified the new Constitution, replacing the Articles of Confederation.
cause: Shays' Rebellion and economic instability under the Articles revealed the need for stronger central authority.
effect: Created the federal system with separation of powers that remains the framework of American government.
causes: Economic chaos and Shays' Rebellion demonstrated the Articles' failures
Commercial interests demanded a stable national currency and trade rules
effects: Created a federal government with the power to tax, regulate commerce, and enforce laws
Established the separation of powers and checks and balances
significance: Created the world's oldest surviving written national constitution
Defined the balance between federal authority and states' rights that still shapes American politics

title: Bill of Rights Ratified
description: The first ten amendments to the Constitution guaranteed individual liberties and limited federal power.
cause: Anti-Federalists demanded explicit protections for individual rights as a condition of ratification.
effect: Established foundational civil liberties that shaped American law and culture.
causes: Anti-Federalists feared a powerful central government would trample individual freedoms
Several states made ratification contingent on adding a bill of rights
effects: Guaranteed fundamental freedoms including speech, religion, and due process
Became the constitutional foundation for civil rights claims across American history
significance: Defined the relationship between the individual and the federal government
Provided legal tools for expanding rights across subsequent centuries

title: Louisiana Purchase
description: The United States purchased approximately 828,000 square miles from France, doubling the nation's size.
cause: Napoleon's military setbacks in Haiti and ambitions in Europe made him eager to sell French North American territory.
effect: Fueled westward expansion, intensified debates over slavery's extension, and raised constitutional questions about presidential power.
causes: Napoleon abandoned his American empire after the Haitian Revolution crushed his army
Jefferson sought control of the Mississippi River and New Orleans for western trade
effects: Doubled the size of the United States
Intensified debates over whether slavery would expand into new territories
significance: Greatest territorial acquisition in American history, enabling westward expansion
Raised unresolved questions about slavery in new territories that would haunt the nation for decades

title: War of 1812
description: The United States declared war on Britain over impressment of sailors and British support for Native American resistance.
cause: British violations of American neutrality and impressment of American sailors inflamed public opinion.
effect: Fostered American nationalism and effectively ended significant Native American resistance east of the Mississippi.
causes: British impressment of American sailors into the Royal Navy
British support for Native American confederacies led by Tecumseh threatening U.S. expansion
effects: Sparked an era of American nationalism (the 'Era of Good Feelings')
Destroyed the pan-Indian resistance movement east of the Mississippi after Tecumseh's death
significance: Consolidated U.S. sovereignty and ended British interference in American affairs
Marked the end of viable Native American resistance to U.S. expansion in the East

title: Missouri Compromise
description: Congress admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, drawing a line at 36°30'.
cause: Missouri's application for statehood as a slave state threatened the balance of free and slave states in the Senate.
effect: Temporarily settled the slavery expansion debate but established a precedent that would be revisited by later crises.
causes: Missouri's 1819 statehood application threatened to tip the Senate balance toward slave states
Northerners feared the political power of expanding slaveholder representation
effects: Preserved sectional balance in the Senate for three decades
Drew the 36°30' line as a geographic boundary for slavery's expansion
significance: Demonstrated that slavery was becoming the central, unresolvable fault line in American politics
Established the pattern of legislative compromise that delayed but could not prevent civil war

title: Indian Removal Act
description: Congress authorized the forced relocation of Native American tribes from the Southeast to lands west of the Mississippi.
cause: White settlers demanded fertile southeastern land and the federal government prioritized expansion over Native rights.
effect: Led to the Trail of Tears and the displacement and deaths of tens of thousands of Native Americans.
causes: Discovery of gold in Cherokee territory in Georgia intensified settler demand for Native land
Jackson's political philosophy rejected federal protection of Native sovereignty
effects: Forced removal of the Five Civilized Tribes in the Trail of Tears, killing thousands
Cleared millions of acres for cotton cultivation and slavery's expansion
significance: Represents a defining episode of ethnic cleansing in American history
Established federal precedent for violating treaty obligations with Native nations

title: Seneca Falls Convention
description: The first women's rights convention produced the Declaration of Sentiments demanding equality for women.
cause: Women reformers, many active in abolition, began applying democratic ideals to their own exclusion from public life.
effect: Launched the organized women's suffrage movement that culminated in the 19th Amendment in 1920.
causes: Women abolitionists were excluded from speaking at the 1840 World Anti-Slavery Convention
Reformers like Stanton applied the ideals of democracy to women's legal and political exclusion
effects: Created the first formal organization for women's rights in America
Launched a 72-year campaign for women's suffrage culminating in the 19th Amendment
significance: Marked the beginning of the organized women's rights movement in the United States
Applied the principles of the Declaration of Independence to argue for women's equality

title: Compromise of 1850
description: A series of acts admitted California as a free state and strengthened the Fugitive Slave Law.
cause: California's application for statehood after the Mexican-American War reignited the slavery extension debate.
effect: Temporarily delayed disunion but the Fugitive Slave Act intensified Northern opposition to slavery.
causes: California's gold rush population demanded statehood as a free state
Southern states demanded protections for slavery to balance the new free state
effects: The Fugitive Slave Act forced Northerners to participate in slavery enforcement
Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote Uncle Tom's Cabin in direct response
significance: Represented the last major sectional compromise before the Civil War
The Fugitive Slave Act converted many Northerners from indifference to active opposition to slavery

title: Kansas-Nebraska Act
description: Congress repealed the Missouri Compromise and allowed popular sovereignty to determine slavery in new territories.
cause: Senator Stephen Douglas wanted to organize territories for a transcontinental railroad and proposed popular sovereignty.
effect: Led to 'Bleeding Kansas,' destroyed the Whig Party, and gave rise to the Republican Party.
causes: Douglas needed Southern support to organize the Nebraska territory for a northern railroad route
Popular sovereignty was his proposed compromise to avoid the Missouri Compromise line
effects: Bleeding Kansas turned the territory into a violent battleground between pro- and anti-slavery settlers
Destroyed the Whig Party and gave rise to the Republican Party
significance: Reopened the question of slavery's expansion that the Missouri Compromise had settled for 34 years
Directly led to the creation of the Republican Party and set the stage for Lincoln's rise

title: Dred Scott Decision
description: The Supreme Court ruled that African Americans were not citizens and Congress could not ban slavery in territories.
cause: Dred Scott sued for his freedom after living in free territories with his enslaved status intact.
effect: Outraged Northerners, emboldened Southerners, and pushed the nation closer to civil war.
causes: Scott argued that residing in free territories made him legally free
Abolitionists backed the case to challenge the constitutionality of slavery
effects: Declared the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional, inflaming Northern opinion
Effectively declared that slavery could spread to all territories, making compromise impossible
significance: Widely considered one of the worst Supreme Court decisions in history
Pushed the nation irrevocably toward civil war by removing the possibility of legislative compromise on slavery

title: Emancipation Proclamation
description: President Lincoln declared enslaved people in Confederate states to be free as a war measure.
cause: Lincoln sought to weaken the Confederacy, energize Union troops, and deter European intervention on the South's behalf.
effect: Transformed the Civil War into a war for freedom and enabled African Americans to enlist in the Union Army.
causes: Military setbacks made Lincoln willing to use emancipation as a war strategy
Britain and France were considering recognizing the Confederacy; Lincoln wanted to make slavery the central issue
effects: Nearly 180,000 African Americans served in the Union Army
Prevented Britain and France from formally recognizing the Confederacy
significance: Transformed the Civil War's purpose from union to freedom
Paved the way for the 13th Amendment and the end of slavery

title: 14th Amendment Ratified
description: The amendment granted citizenship to formerly enslaved people and guaranteed equal protection under the law.
cause: Congress sought to enshrine the Civil Rights Act of 1866 in the Constitution to protect freedpeople's rights.
effect: Became the constitutional basis for civil rights decisions throughout the 20th century and beyond.
causes: Southern states passed Black Codes to effectively re-enslave freedpeople after the war
Congress needed constitutional protection for Black citizenship that could not be repealed by statute
effects: Overturned Dred Scott by granting citizenship to all born in the U.S.
Became the foundation for most 20th-century civil rights and civil liberties decisions
significance: Most important constitutional amendment since the Bill of Rights
The basis of nearly all modern civil rights law, from school desegregation to same-sex marriage

title: Transcontinental Railroad Completed
description: The Central Pacific and Union Pacific railroads met at Promontory Summit, Utah, connecting the continent by rail.
cause: The federal government funded construction to bind the nation together and facilitate western settlement.
effect: Accelerated industrialization, enabled mass western migration, and devastated Native American peoples and bison herds.
causes: Federal government issued land grants and loans to incentivize private railroad construction
Post-Civil War leaders saw a continental railroad as essential to national unity and economic growth
effects: Enabled mass settlement of the Great Plains, displacing Native American nations
Fueled industrial capitalism by integrating national markets
significance: Transformed the American economy by creating a truly national market
Accelerated the destruction of Native American cultures and bison herds of the Great Plains

title: Sherman Antitrust Act
description: Congress passed the first federal law to limit monopolies and protect competitive markets.
cause: Public outrage over Standard Oil, railroads, and other trusts that fixed prices and crushed competition.
effect: Established the legal framework for antitrust enforcement, though weakly applied until the Progressive Era.
causes: The Gilded Age saw massive monopolistic trusts control oil, steel, and railroads
Farmers and small businesses demanded federal protection from price manipulation
effects: Created the legal basis for breaking up monopolies, though rarely enforced until TR
Gave future presidents a tool to challenge corporate power
significance: First federal recognition that unregulated capitalism could harm the public interest
Laid the groundwork for the Progressive Era's trust-busting reforms

title: Spanish-American War
description: The U.S. defeated Spain in a brief war, gaining Guam, Puerto Rico, and the Philippines.
cause: Yellow journalism, the sinking of the USS Maine, and Cuban rebels' struggle for independence rallied U.S. public opinion.
effect: Launched the United States as an imperial power with overseas territories and global military commitments.
causes: Yellow journalism by Hearst and Pulitzer inflamed public opinion against Spain
American business interests in Cuba and strategic interest in Pacific trade routes
effects: U.S. acquired its first overseas empire: Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines
Sparked the Philippine-American War as Filipinos resisted American colonialism
significance: Marked the United States' emergence as a global imperial power
Created ongoing moral debates about American colonialism that echo today

title: 19th Amendment Ratified
description: Women gained the constitutional right to vote in all U.S. elections.
cause: Decades of suffragist organizing, women's wartime service in WWI, and President Wilson's belated support.
effect: Enfranchised millions of women, though literacy tests and poll taxes continued to block many women of color.
causes: 72 years of suffragist organizing since Seneca Falls (1848)
Women's massive contributions to the World War I effort strengthened the case for suffrage
effects: Enfranchised approximately 26 million women
Literacy tests and poll taxes still prevented most Southern Black women from voting
significance: Largest single expansion of voting rights in American history
Demonstrated that sustained organized activism could achieve constitutional change

title: New Deal Begins
description: FDR launched sweeping federal programs to provide relief, recovery, and reform during the Great Depression.
cause: The Great Depression left a quarter of Americans unemployed and previous administrations' laissez-faire policies had failed.
effect: Permanently expanded the federal government's role in the economy and created the modern social safety net.
causes: 25% unemployment and massive bank failures demanded unprecedented government intervention
Hoover's laissez-faire approach failed to stop the economic collapse
effects: Created Social Security, the FDIC, the SEC, and other lasting federal institutions
Established the Democratic coalition of labor, minorities, and liberals that dominated politics for decades
significance: Fundamentally redefined the relationship between the federal government and American citizens
Created the modern regulatory state and social safety net that still exists today

title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
description: Japan's surprise attack on the U.S. naval base brought America into World War II.
cause: Japan sought to neutralize American naval power while it expanded its empire in Asia and the Pacific.
effect: United American public opinion behind the war effort and brought the U.S. into WWII the following day.
causes: U.S. oil embargo threatened Japan's imperial expansion in Asia
Japan calculated that a preemptive strike would cripple U.S. naval response
effects: Ended American isolationism and unified public opinion for war
Led to the forced internment of Japanese Americans under Executive Order 9066
significance: Ended U.S. isolationism and transformed America into the world's dominant military power
The internment of Japanese Americans remains one of the most significant civil liberties violations in U.S. history

title: Brown v. Board of Education
description: The Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional.
cause: NAACP lawyers, led by Thurgood Marshall, challenged separate-but-equal schooling as inherently unequal.
effect: Overturned Plessy v. Ferguson and accelerated the Civil Rights Movement by legitimizing integration.
causes: NAACP pursued a deliberate legal strategy to dismantle Jim Crow through the courts
Psychologist Kenneth Clark's doll experiments showed the psychological harm of segregation
effects: Overturned Plessy v. Ferguson's 'separate but equal' doctrine
Galvanized the Civil Rights Movement and triggered massive resistance in the South
significance: Most consequential Supreme Court decision of the 20th century
Demonstrated that the 14th Amendment could be used as a tool for racial equality

title: Civil Rights Act of 1964
description: Landmark legislation outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.
cause: Televised brutality against peaceful protesters and the assassination of JFK created political will for reform.
effect: Prohibited employment discrimination and segregation in public places, transforming American society.
causes: Televised footage of Bull Connor's fire hoses and police dogs in Birmingham shocked the nation
LBJ used JFK's assassination to push for the stalled civil rights bill
effects: Outlawed segregation in public accommodations and employment discrimination
Created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC)
significance: Most comprehensive civil rights legislation since Reconstruction
Extended protections to women and other minorities beyond race
